p.seg: it is not something that inferior scholars can hear,
how can shallow knowledge fathom it!
The "Zi" (Master) that is spoken of,
is a respectful title for those who have virtue,
in ancient times, teachers were called "Zi".
It is also said that "Zi" is the title of the book,
not just the collective name for three sections,
but also a common title for the hundred schools of thought.
As for what is meant by "Inner Chapters,"
"Inner" is named in relation to "Outer," to establish a distinction.
"Chapter" (篇) means a collection of bamboo slips arranged together.
In ancient times, they scraped bamboo to make slips,
and used leather to bind them.
Arranging the slips creates a chapter,
just as connecting sheets of paper today creates a scroll.
Therefore, Yuan Kai said:
"Important matters are recorded on bamboo tablets,
while minor matters are recorded on simple slips."
"Inner" discusses fundamental principles,
while "Outer" speaks of events and traces.
Though events are clearly visible,
they cannot be understood without principle;
though principles are profound and subtle,
they cannot be revealed without events.
Wanting to first clarify the subtle principles,
therefore, we first present the Inner Chapters.
The Inner Chapters contain profound principles,
therefore, we separately establish the titles of each chapter outside the main text.
Guō Xiàng 郭象 still annotated directly beneath the titles,
such as "Xiāoyáo" 逍遙 and "Qíwù" 齊物.
From the outer chapters onwards,
he took the first two characters of the chapter to be its title,
such as "Piánmǔ" 駢拇 and "Mǎtí" 馬蹄.

Preface to Zhuāngzǐ
Written by Guō Xiàng Zǐxuán of Hénán
Now, Zhuāngzǐ,
can be said to have understood the root.
Therefore, he never concealed his wild words,
words that, though not calculated, are uniquely responsive.
Now, to be responsive without calculation,
is to be useless even if correct.
If words do not concern material affairs,
they cannot be put into practice, no matter how lofty.
This is quite different from being silent and still,
and only arising when absolutely necessary.
There is indeed a separation,
This can be called understanding the one who has no mind.
For if the mind is without action,
then it responds to stimuli.
The response follows the time,
words are only cautious.
Therefore, he unites with transformation,
flows through ten thousand generations, and merges with things,
how could he have ever set up opposition, encountered things in isolation, and roamed and talked outside the realm?
This is why it is not canonical yet is the crown of the hundred schools.
However, although Zhuāng Shēng did not embody it,
his words are ultimate.
He understands the unifying principle of Heaven and Earth,
orders the nature of all things,
comprehends the transformations of life and death,
and elucidates the way of inner sage and outer king.
Above, he knows the Creator has no thing;
below, he knows things create themselves.
His words are vast and generous,
his purpose profound and subtle.
The ultimate Way,
blends subtle meaning with elegance;
calm and unrestrained,
unrestrained without arrogance.
Therefore, it is said that he does not know where righteousness leads,
wildly and recklessly acting and treading upon the Great Square;
holding food in his mouth, he rejoices in indifference,
drumming his belly, he wanders in chaos (1).
Ultimate benevolence reaches a state of impartiality,
filial piety and kindness ultimately reach mutual forgetting,
rites and music revert to what is already capable,
loyalty and trustworthiness emanate from heavenly light.
Use its light, and its uncarved nature will naturally be complete.
Therefore, the divine implement transforms alone in the realm of profound darkness, and its source flows deep and long (3).
Therefore, what the long wave washes away,
what its high winds fan,
thoroughly suits the appropriateness of things,
and fits the desires of the people.
Broaden their narrowness,
resolve their doubts,
even without the application of purifying effort,
the grounds for pride and boasting dissipate.
Therefore, reading his book,
one surpassingly feels that he has already attained,
passing through Kunlun,
traversing the great void,
and wandering in the courts of elusiveness.
Even avaricious people,
impetuous scholars,
if they but briefly grasp its lingering fragrance,
taste its overflowing current,
and vaguely perceive its sounds and shadows,
are still sufficiently enlightened to have a feeling of forgetting their form and attaining self-satisfaction.
How much more so for those who explore its distant meaning and savor eternal life!
Thus, one extends far into the clear distance,
leaves behind the dust of the world, and returns to the ultimate darkness.
【Corrections】 (One) The character "芒" (máng, awn) in the Song dynasty Zhao Jianyi version is written as "茫" (máng, vast).
(Two) The character "仁" (rén, benevolence) is corrected according to the ancient Yi Congshu reprint of the Song version.
(Three) "源流深長" (yuánliú shēn cháng, the source is deep and the flow is long) in the Zhao Jianyi version is written as "源深流長" (yuán shēn liú cháng, the source is deep, the flow is long).
Preface to Zhuangzi
Written by Cheng Xuanying, a Tang Dynasty West Hua Dharma Master
Now, Zhuangzi,
is what explains the deep root of morality,
narrates the wondrous essence of profound mystery,
expresses the tranquility of non-action,
illuminates the obscurity of solitary transformation,
restrains the nine schools,
encompasses the hundred schools,
truly is the supreme teaching within the region,
indeed, it is the subtle words beyond phenomena.
The person's surname is Zhuang,
given name Zhou,
courtesy name Zixiu,
born in Meng County, Suiyang, Song State,
studied under Master Changsang,
received the title "Immortal of South Hua".
At the beginning of the Warring States period,
at the end of the declining Zhou dynasty,
lamenting the meager achievements of the people,
grieving the decline of morality,
he thus bravely rose in indignation,
and consequently wrote this treatise.
Its words are vast and broad,
its essence is deep and far-reaching,
has been explained differently throughout ancient and modern times.
Now, I will broadly outline the main points
and briefly offer three interpretations.
These three interpretations are:
First,
Gù Tóngbǎi 顧桐柏 said:
"Xiāo 逍 means
to dissolve;
yáo 遙 means
distant.
Dissolving completely the burden of deliberate action,
and seeing distantly the principle of non-action.
To wander in this way,
is why it is called 'Xiāoyáo.'"
Second,
Zhī Dàolín 支道林 said:
"Managing all things without being managed by them,
therefore one is carefree and doesn't rely on oneself;
profound insight is not hurried yet swift,
therefore one is free and there is nothing one does not do.
Wandering the world in this way,
is why it is called 'Xiāoyáo Yóu.'"
Third,
Mù Yèyún:
"The term 'xiāoyáo'
generally refers to a state of unrestrained freedom and self-contentment.
With inner virtue fully cultivated,
one is comfortable at all times;
he can achieve great equanimity in all realms,
hence 'Qí Wù' (Equalizing Things) follows.
Having indicated the 'horse' (hoof) and heaven and earth,
blending together all things,
the mind is serene and calm,
one can then focus on nurturing life,
hence 'Yǎng Shēng Zhǔ' (Nourishing the Lord of Life) follows.
Having forgotten both good and evil,
and both realms and wisdom are exquisitely subtle,
following changes and yielding to transformations,
one can live and interact within the human world.
Therefore, "The Human World" follows.
Inner virtue is complete,
therefore one can disperse one's virtue,
externally to connect with things.
And then, following the rising and falling of things,
inner and outer (realities) are in silent accord.
Therefore, "Signs of Perfect Virtue" follows.
Still water is a flowing mirror,
connecting with things without intention,
forgetting virtue and forgetting form,
in accord with the ultimate of meeting the outer and uniting with the inner.
One can craft and form the myriad things.
Therefore, "The Great and Venerable Teacher" follows.
The true sages of old,
understood Heaven and understood humanity,
shared the same function as creation,
being both still and responsive.
Thereafter, he drove and directed the myriad things,
therefore, he followed up with "Responding to Emperors and Kings."
"Webbed Fingers" and following chapters,
all take the first two characters of the chapter as the title,
and have no other meaning,
so I will not discuss those chapters again.
But from ancient times, noble scholars,
recluses of the Jin and Han dynasties,
all never failed to admire and study it,
and to create explanations for it;
although there are no flaws in the commentaries and explanations,
and there are beautiful words,
all are able to seek out the hidden meanings.
Xuányīng, disregarding his own ordinariness and dullness,
learned it from a young age,
and has been diligently studying and deeply contemplating it for thirty years.
Based on the thirty chapters commented on by Zǐ Xuán,
he has thus written a commentary,
totaling thirty scrolls.
Although the wording is clumsy and unskilled,
it still has somewhat of a direction and destination for the heart and mind;
I dare not leave it to later generations,
but simply record it for my own remembrance of what I might forget.
【Correction】 (1) The character "蹄" (tí, hoof) is also erroneously added in the replicated Song edition,
according to the meaning of the "Equality of Things" chapter, "Heaven and earth are one finger,
all things are one horse," it should be deleted.
Preface to the Collected Interpretations of Zhuangzi
Guō Jūnzǐ completed the Collected Interpretations of Zhuangzi,
And gave it to Xiānqiān to read,
and that year happened to have the Dongyi rebellion,
and (he) rose and sighed, saying:
Zhuāngzǐ must have had some compelling reason in his heart!
For he encountered a world of blockage and obstruction,
and there was no way to salvage it,
his spirit wandered in the vastness,
examining the boundlessness of small and large,
investigating the beginning and end of heaven and earth,
and in fear made these words.
Zōu Yǎn said:
"What the Confucians call the Middle Kingdom,
in the world is only one of eighty-one parts.
Outside the Red County Divine Province, there are nine continents,
surrounded by a coastal sea,
and the great ocean surrounds them."
Huì Shī said:
"I know the center of the world,
it is north of Yān,
and south of Yuè."
And Zhuāngzǐ praised them,
and also spoke of Shū and Hū drilling the chaos to death,
his words seem to foresee the future and infer its ultimate end,
truly a different person!
Zǐgòng made a shadoof for drawing water,
and the old man of Hànyīn laughed at him.
Today's mechanical devices and contraptions,
are ten thousand times greater than the shadoof.
If you were to have Zhuangzi see this,
what would he say?
The Mán and Chù clans fight over territory on a snail's horn,
resulting in tens of thousands of corpses,
chasing the defeated for ten days.
The Mán and Chù clans of today are countless in number,
so what could Zhuangzi do?
Therefore, even with the Yellow Emperor as ruler, there was Chiyou,
and with Yao as ruler, there were Congzhi, Zong, Kuai, and Xu Ao.
The Yellow Emperor and Yao were not fond of such affairs,
yet they wanted to empty their state
and punish their people.
It was decisively clear
that they could not govern with emptiness and stillness.
That Zhuangzi,
seeking his methods but failing to find them,
will then go on to live alone in the vast wilderness,
hoping to preserve his life and enjoy his existence,
how can he possibly concern himself with the world!
Moreover, his writings have long been exposed to later generations.
The Jin dynasty developed them into metaphysics,
which offered no solution to the chaos of the barbarian Hu and Jie tribes;
the Tang dynasty revered them as true scriptures,
which provided no salvation from the An Lushan Rebellion.
They merely serve to intoxicate rulers with indulgence and extravagance,
and dilute the common people's pursuit of profit and desire,
perhaps offering a slight bit of help in one or two instances.
And his writing is exceptionally remarkable,
Guō Jūn loved playing with it endlessly,
thus, he had a compilation and interpretation made,
appending it with prose,
enriching it with broad knowledge.
If Zhuāngzǐ saw it,
wouldn't he say, "This is just my dregs and leavings"?
However,
without footprints, how can one measure the shoe,
without dregs and leavings, how can one observe the ancient beauty!
Therefore, Master Guō wrote this book to be a subsidiary to ink,
intending that all under heaven become descendants who recite it in the style of Luò!
In the twelfth month of winter, in the year Jiǎwǔ, the twentieth year of Guangxu (光緒),
respectfully written by your foolish younger brother from Chángshā, Wáng Xiānqiān.

◎ Qìngfān notes, Liú Yìqìng's *Shìshuō Xīnyǔ*, Literary category, says:
"Zhuāngzǐ's Free and Easy Wandering chapter,
was formerly a difficult point;
something that the various famous worthies could delve into,
but could not extract a principle beyond that of Guō Xiàng.
Zhī Dàolín, at the White Horse Temple,
was conversing with Féng Tàicháng,
and the discussion reached carefree wandering.
Zhī strikingly marked out a new principle beyond the two families,
establishing a different meaning beyond the various worthies,
all of which were things the various famous worthies sought to understand but could not,
and later they adopted Zhī's principle."
Liú Xiàobiāo's commentary says:
"Xiàng Zǐqī and Guō Zǐxuán's explanation of carefree wandering says:
'The great Peng bird soars to ninety thousand *lǐ*,
while the little sparrow rises to the elm and sandalwood trees;
although the small and great differ,
each fulfills its nature.
If each is fulfilling their lot,
that is also carefree wandering.
However, the myriad things,
all rely on something to depend on.
Only by obtaining what they depend on,
can they then be carefree.
Only the sage merges with things and follows the great changes,
Is able to be without reliance and constantly connected.
How could it be merely self-connected!
Moreover, those who depend on something do not lose what they depend on,
not losing it is equivalent to great connection."
Zhī's Discussion on Untrammeled Wandering says:
"Now, untrammeled wandering,
illuminates the mind of the perfect person.
Zhuāng Shēng established words on the Great Dao,
and metaphorically referred to the *peng* bird and the sparrow.
The *peng* bird, because its path of survival is vast,
therefore loses comfort to things external to itself;
the sparrow, because it is near and laughs at the distance,
has self-importance and boasting within its mind.
The perfect person rides the heavenly correctness and enjoys high spirits,
wandering endlessly in abandonment.
He deals with things, but is not dealt with by things,
and thus wanders freely, not finding himself constrained;
his profound response is non-doing,
not quick but swift,
and thus he wanders freely, not failing to be comfortable.
This is the reason for being untrammeled and free.
As for having desires that meet their fulfillment,
fulfilled in what is fulfilled,
happily resembling innate nature,
it is like a hungry person having one full meal,
a thirsty person having one full drink.
How could they forget the seasonal sacrifices for dried provisions,
cut off the wine cups for fermented drinks!
If one is not perfectly self-sufficient,
how can one be considered free and unfettered!"
This is what Xiàng Guō's commentary did not fully explore.
@[Explanatory Notes] [逍] pronounced xiāo,
also written as 消.
[遙] as the character itself indicates.
Also written as 搖.
◎Qìng Fān's note: The two characters 逍遙,
are not included in the Shuōwén dictionary;
it is correct to write them as 消搖.
In the Book of Rites, Tán Gōng chapter: "wandering idly at the door";
In the History of the Han Dynasty, Biography of Sīmǎ Xiàngrú: "wandering idly in Xiāng Yáng";
Jīng Shān quotes from the Classic of the Mystery, "Even if the united heads wish to be free and unfettered,
Heaven will not allow it";
On the stone pillars of the Kaìmǔ Shrine of the Hàn Dynasty, it is written: "Adorned with brilliance and freedom";
In the Selections of Literature, Sòng Yù's "Nine Arguments": "I will idly wander in contemplation";
In the History of the Later Hàn, Biography of Dōngpíng Xiàn Wáng Cāng: "wandering idly in contemplation";
The characters are all written with the water radical for 消,
and the hand radical for 搖.
In the Táng Dynasty, Buddhist monk Zhànrán's Auxiliary Conduct for the Cessation and Contemplation, Hóng Jué quotes Wáng Mào saying at night:
"消搖 means,
the idea of being harmoniously carefree and leisurely."
Indeed, perfect principle is sufficient within;
there is no time when it is not suitable;
focusing the mind on responding to things;
there is nowhere it does not penetrate.
By this, one travels the world;
therefore it is called 消搖.
Furthermore, it is said:
The principle (lǐ) has no hidden depths,
It vanishes yet is fitting,
Form has no great or small,
It sways yet is all-pervading,
therefore it is called *xiāo yáo*.
Explaining the meaning of *xiāo yáo*,
[Zhuāngzǐ] surpasses all scholars.
*Yóu* [遊] is as the character [is].
It is also written as *yóu* [游].
*Xiāo Yáo Yóu* [逍遙遊],
is the name of the chapter,
Its meaning is taken to be leisurely and unrestrained,
Cheerful and content.
◎ Qìng Fān observes: My late father, Minister of the Household, said:
In the *Tiān Xià* chapter, Zhuāngzǐ speaks of his doctrine and arts as substantial and inexhaustible,
and he roams above with the Creator.
The first chapter is entitled *Xiāo Yáo Yóu*,
Zhuāngzǐ uses its boundless words to describe himself.
The commentary says that although small and great are different,
*xiāo yáo* is the same [for both].
This seems to miss the point of Zhuāngzǐ.
◎ Furthermore, in the annotation to Pān Ānrén's "Autumn Excursion Ode" in the *Wén Xuǎn*, it quotes Sīmǎ Biāo saying:
Speaking of *xiāo yáo wú wéi*, it means being able to roam the Great Dao.

【Commentary】 *Míng*,
is similar to "sea,"
taking from it the boundless and limitless vastness,
therefore (called) [it is called] = "called" was often confused in ancient times,
now it is distinguished by meaning.
It will not appear again.
= of *Míng*.
*Dōngfāng Shuò*'s *Shí Zhōu Jì* says:
"The *Míng* sea has no wind, yet its vast waves are a hundred *zhàng* high."
Within this giant sea,
there is this large fish.
Intending to clarify that the nature of things is natural,
therefore it is marked as the chapter's beginning.
*Xuán Zhōng Jì* says:
"In the east, there is a large fish,
a traveler takes one day to pass its head,
and seven days to pass its tail;
during the three days of spawning,
the azure sea turns red because of it."
Therefore, know that large things are born in large places,
not only in the Northern Sea.
@【Textual Explanation】 "běi míng" originally also written as "míng",
"Mì jīng fǎn" refers to,
the North Sea.
Jī Kāng said:
"It is named so for its dark and boundless expanse."
Emperor Jiǎnwén of the Liáng Dynasty said:
"It is deep and limitless,
therefore it is called 'Míng' (dark)."
The *Shí Zhōu Jì* (Record of the Ten Continents) by Dōngfāng Shuò says:
"Water of black color is called the Dark Sea (Mínghǎi),
with huge waves of a hundred *zhàng* high even without wind."

( [Transforming into a bird,
its name is 鵬 (péng).])
[Commentary] As for the reality of 鵬 (péng) and 鲲 (kūn),
I am not sure about it.
The general idea of Zhuāngzǐ lies
in unfettered and unrestrained wandering,
achieving self-possession through non-action.
Therefore, he exhausts the extremes of small and large to clarify the suitability of one's nature and destiny.
Enlightened scholars
should grasp the ultimate meaning and disregard the vehicles of expression.
It is not necessary to meticulously argue with his explanations in every detail.
As long as it does not harm the grand purpose,
all such details can be omitted.
@ [Explanation] The four seasons rush by like wind,
the sun, moon, and stars flash like lightning.
Therefore, they bear mountains on their backs and abandon the old,
and raise boats in valleys to pursue the new.
Hence, the transformation of a fish into a bird
is intended to illustrate the grand principle of change.
@ [Textual Explanation] 《鵬》 (Péng): bù dēng fǎn.
Xú's pronunciation is péng.
Guō's pronunciation is fǔ dēng fǎn.
Cuī's pronunciation is fèng,
saying:
鵬 (péng) is actually the ancient character for 鳳 (fèng),
not the 鳳 (fèng) that comes to offer tribute.
Shuōwén (說文) says:
"朋 (péng)" and "鵬 (péng)"
are both ancient forms of the character 鳳 (fèng).

The Inner Chapters clarify fundamental principles,

From here on down to Lièzǐ,
the text lists the different sizes of life-span,
each believing in its own perspective,
none being able to overrule the others.
Then it sums it up with the person who is "without-dependency,"
abandoning both self and others,
obscuring the differences among all things,
arriving equally from differing perspectives while I have no merit or fame.
Therefore, one who encompasses both small and large
is neither small nor large.
If one possesses a concept of size,
then even the great Pèng bird and the small chìyàn,
the official and the rider of the wind,
Both are burdens.
Those who equalize death and life
have neither death nor life;
if there is truly death and life,
then even the great *chūn* tree and the cicada,
*Péng Zǔ* and the morning glory mushroom,
are all equal in being short-lived.
Therefore, to wander in that which is neither small nor large
is to be without end;
to be in the darkness of neither dying nor living
is to be without limit.
If one roams freely but is tied to a direction,
then even if one is allowed to roam freely, there will still be an end,
and one will still be dependent on something.
@[Commentary] Living things receive different *qì*,
and their endowments differ;
their intelligence is either bright or dim,
and their lifespans are either short or long.
Thus, consider the morning glory mushroom, the dark turtle, and the officer Róng Zǐ,
all of which resemble lifespans,
how can yearning and aspiring reach them!
Therefore, knowing that the natures of things are different,
one should not forcibly try to emulate each other.

【Three】【Commentary】 This answers the previous question.
*Zhāo Jūn* (morning mushroom),
refers to when the weather is continuously rainy,
and they are born from the hot steam above manure piles.
They are born in damp and shady places,
and die when exposed to the sun.
They are also called *Dà Zhī* (large fungus).
They are born in the morning and die in the evening,
hence they are called *Zhāo Jūn*.
The end of the month is called *huì* (晦),
the beginning of the month is called *shuò* (朔);
Supposing there is continuous shade,
they will wither in a few days,
and will certainly not last thirty days,
therefore they do not know the *huì shuò*.
*Huì Gū*,
is the summer cicada.
They are born from wheat stalks,
also called *Mài Jié* (wheat node).
Those born in summer and die in autumn,
therefore, do not know spring and autumn.
The *jùn* mushroom is born in the morning and dies in the evening,
the cicada grows in summer and perishes in autumn.
These speak of a short lifespan,
hence they are called "small years."

◎Qìngfān's [慶藩] note: The phrase "ér zhēng yī guó" [而徵一國] (and establish a state),
The commentary and Guō's [郭] annotation offer no interpretation.
The Cheng [成] commentary reads "ér" [而] as a transitional particle,
which is incorrect.
The character "ér" [而] should be read as "néng" [能] (to be able to),
Néng (能) and ér (而) have similar ancient pronunciations and were used interchangeably.
Guān (官), xiāng (鄉), jūn (君), and guó (國) are in opposition;
zhī (知), rén (仁), dé (德), and néng (能) are also in opposition;
therefore, it is clear that the character ér (而) is not a transitional word.
In the "Yuán Dào" (原道) chapter of the *Huáinánzǐ* (淮南子), it says, "ér (而) takes the few and makes them many."
Gāo's (高) commentary states:
"Ér (而)
means néng (能)."
The commentaries on the "Qù Sī" (去私) and "Bù Qū" (不屈) chapters of the *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* (呂氏春秋) all say:
"Ér (而)
means néng (能)."
In the "Shàng Tóng" (尚同) chapter of the *Mòzǐ* (墨子), it says:
"Therefore, the ancient sage kings only néng (而) carefully prioritized agreement to establish correct leaders."
It also says:
"What is the reason for order in the world?
It is only néng (而) by prioritizing agreement that one governs."
In the "Fēi Mìng" (非命) chapter, it says:
"Not néng (而) correcting the desires of their ears and eyes."
In the *Chǔ Cí* (楚辭) "Jiǔ Zhāng" (九章), it says:
"In this world, who néng (而) knows it?"
In the *Qí Cè* (齊策), it says:
"Who néng (而) will go with me to meet the feudal lords?"
Ér (而) is used synonymously with néng (能).
In the *Yáodiǎn* (堯典), it says, "Comforting those far away and néng (能) approaching those near."
The inscription on the *Hàn Dūyóu Bān Bēi* (漢督郵班碑) renders it as ér (而) for approaching those near.
In the *Gāoyáo Mó* (皋陶謨), it says, "Néng (能) wise and ér (而) benevolent."
The *Wèi Wèi Héng Fāng Bēi* (衛尉衡方碑) renders it as néng (能) wise and néng (能) benevolent.
The *Shǐjì Xià Běnjì* (史記夏本記) renders it as néng (能) wise, intelligent, and benevolent.
*Lǐ Yùn Zhèngyì* says:

【12】 【Commentary】If there is no wind, it cannot travel,
thus there must be reliance;
only those who ride on everything have no reliance.
@ 【Subcommentary】Riding the wind to lift up lightly,
although avoiding walking,
without wind it cannot advance,
still it has a need for reliance.
From the officials downwards, and including Sòng Róng Yù Kòu,
listing intelligence and virtue with differing strengths and weaknesses,
since they have not forgotten everything,
all return to having reliance.
Only when according with the nature of all things,
travelling the path of change,
and being able to accomplish everything,
can one fully exhaust the wondrous attainment of carefree wandering.
【13】 【Commentary】Heaven and Earth are
the collective name for all things.
Heaven and Earth take all things as their body,
and all things must take nature as their standard,
nature is
that which is natural without being contrived.
Therefore, the great *péng* bird is able to fly high,
the small swallow is able to fly low,
the *chūn* tree is able to grow long,
the morning mushroom is able to grow short,
all of this is what nature is able to do,
not what contrivance is able to do.
Able to do without contriving,
This is what is meant by being correct.
Therefore, to ride the correctness of Heaven and Earth
is to accord with the nature of all things.
To control the variations of the six *qì*
is to roam the path of transformation.
If one proceeds in this manner,
then where can one go that has an end?
Whatever one encounters, one rides;
then what else would one need to wait for?
This is the carefree wandering of a person of supreme virtue, who mysteriously identifies with both self and other.
If one has something to rely on,
then even with Lièzǐ's Lie Zi's lightness and subtlety,
he still cannot travel without wind.
Thus, he must obtain what he relies on
before he can wander freely,
how much more so the great *Péng* bird!
Only those who merge with things and follow great transformations
are able to be free from reliance and always flow,
how could they just pass through of themselves?
Furthermore, it is to accord with those who have dependencies,
so that they do not lose what they rely on.
If what they rely on is not lost,
then it is the same as great passage.
Therefore, having dependencies and not having dependencies
are things I cannot equate.
As for each being at peace with its nature,
and the heavenly mechanism unfolding on its own,
receiving without knowing,
zé wú suǒ bù néng shū yě. Then that is something I cannot differentiate.
fú wú dài yóu bù zú yǐ shū yǒu dài, Indeed, that which is without dependence is still not enough to differentiate that which is dependent,
kuàng yǒu dài zhě zhī jù xì hū! how much more so the great and small of those which are dependent!

◎Qìng Fān's commentary quotes various scholars' explanations of the Six Qi,
each with its own differences.
Sīmǎ takes yin and yang, wind, rain, and darkness (or brightness) as the Six Qi,
which is the oldest explanation.
Lǐ considers dawn, midday, sunset, midnight, and the combination of heaven, black, earth, and yellow as the Six Qi,
which is somewhat far-fetched.
Wáng Yì and Zhī Dùn take heaven, earth, and the four seasons as the Six Qi.
Now, the qi of heaven and earth
is immeasurably vast,
and the four seasons all receive the qi of heaven and earth to form their qi,
so it seems inappropriate to list the four seasons alongside heaven and earth as the Six.
Wáng Yīnglín says:
the Six Qi are,
Lesser Yin Sovereign Fire,
Greater Yin Damp Earth,
Lesser Yang Minister Fire,
Yang Brightness Dry Metal,
Greater Yang Cold Water,
and Terminal Yin Wind Wood,
and fire alone has two.
Heaven uses six as its measure,
therefore the qi uses six cycles to complete one cycle.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* relates the words of Yī Hé,
that heaven has six qi,
(comment says:
yin and yang, wind, rain, darkness (obscurity) [brightness].)
These descend and produce the five flavors.
This is the same as the numbers five and six in the *Sù Wèn* (*The Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic*).
(Quán Zǔwàng says:
Heaven is five, earth (five) [six] (four),
seen in the *Great Change* (*I Ching*),
Heaven is six, earth is five,
seen in the *Discourses of the States* (*Guó Yǔ*).
[Therefore, the (Fifth) *Book of Han* says,
five and six combine at the center of heaven and earth.
However, the *Zuǒ's* explanation
is also different from the *Sù Wèn*.)

With regard to its manifestation in humans, it is the kidneys.
The kidneys are two:

the right is Shǎoyáng Xiànghuǒ (少 陽 相 火, Lesser Yang Ministerial Fire).

The central Tài (Yīn) Tǔ (太 （陰） 土, Greater (Yin) Earth) is the Gōuchén (句 陳, a star),
paired with the spleen.
The explanations of the Six Qì (六 氣, Six Energies)
are chaotic and contentious,
with no consensus.
I believe there are two explanations:
First,
the "Hong Fan" (洪 範, Great Plan) speaks of rain, sunshine, heat, cold, and wind as the Six Qì.
Rain
is wood;
sunshine
is metal;
heat
is fire;
cold
is water;
wind
is earth.
These are the Five Qì.
When the Five Qì are timely,
they are the harmonious Qì of the Five Elements,
and combined, they become the Six Qì.
Qì can be harmonious or disharmonious.
To go against the norm is to change;
when there is change, one should have something to control it.
Therefore, it is said, "control the changes of the six *qì*."
First,
the six *qì* are the six emotions.
The "Biography of Yì Fèng" in the *Hàn Shū* records that Fèng also quoted a teacher's saying about the six emotions, saying:

is liking.
Liking leads to greedy behavior,

the emotion of the east

Anger leads to treacherous behavior,
governed by hài-mǎo;
the emotion of the south
is dislike.
Dislike leads to corrupt behavior,
governed by yín-wǔ;
the emotion of the west
is joy.
Joy leads to generous behavior,
governed by jǐ-yǒu;
the emotion of above
is happiness.
Happiness leads to deceitful and wicked behavior,
governed by chén-wèi;
the emotion of below
is sorrow.
Pitying actions are impartial,
xu and chǒu govern them.
These two interpretations seem to be able to be taken as reference for comparison.

【一六】【Note】A sage (shèng rén) is merely the name given to things that have attained their nature,

@【Commentary】"Ultimate" (zhì) speaks of its substance (tǐ),
"spirit" (shén) speaks of its function (yòng),
"sage" (shèng) speaks of its name (míng).
Therefore, speaking of substance, we use "ultimate";
speaking of function, we use "spirit";
speaking of name, we use "sage";
in reality, they are one.
Reaching the extreme of the numinous,
hence it is called "ultimate";
unfathomable in terms of Yīn and Yáng,
hence it is called "spirit";
correctly naming the myriad things,
hence it is called "sage."
Above a single person,
there are these three,
intending to make clear that though their merits and uses are different, their names are distinct,
hence there is a distinction of three people.
These three people
are precisely those described earlier as "riding the correctness of Heaven and Earth, and responding to the changes of the six qi."
To expound on this person's virtue of non-reliance,
and to clarify its essence and application,
he says "therefore, it is said."

Yáo offered the world to Xǔ Yóu
saying:
"Now that the sun and moon have risen, for a torch to not be extinguished,
in terms of light,
Is it not difficult!
The timely rain has fallen, yet still one must irrigate.
Regarding the swamps,
is it not laborious!
If the Master were to stand and the world be governed,
yet I still remain in his position,
I view myself as deficient.
I request to relinquish the world."
[Commentary] Yáo
was the son of Dì Kù,
his surname was Yī Qí,
his given name was Fàng Xūn,
his mother was Qìng Dū.
(Kù) was moved by a red dragon and gave birth to him.
He was one zhàng tall,
broad above and full below,
his eyebrows had eight colors,
his feet stepped on the Wing Star,
and he possessed sagely virtue.
At the age of fifteen,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Táng,
at twenty-one,
he succeeded his brother and ascended the throne,
with his capital at Píngyáng,
and his title was Táo Táng.
After seventy-two years on the throne,
he then passed it on to Shùn.
He died at the age of one hundred and twenty-eight,
He was buried in Yángchéng.
His posthumous title was Yáo.
According to the rules for posthumous titles,
"One who skillfully continues goodness and transmits sageliness" is called Yáo,
meaning that he had the merit of passing the throne to Shùn.
Xǔ Yóu
was a recluse.
His surname was Xǔ,
his given name was Yóu,
his style name was Zhòngwǔ,
and he was from Yǐngchuān's Yángchéng.
He lived in seclusion on Mount Jī,
studied under Niè Quē,
ate food obtained from the mountains,
and drank from the river.
Yáo, knowing of his virtue,
offered him the imperial throne.
Xǔ Yóu, upon hearing this,
then went to the river and washed his ears.
Cháo Fǔ, while leading his calf to drink,
pulled it away to avoid the water,
saying,
"I abhor your water!"
After his death,
Yáo honored his grave,
bestowing upon him the posthumous title of Duke Jī,
which is to say, he was a teacher of Yáo.

The governing comes from not governing,
the action comes from non-action.
Taking it from Yáo is sufficient;
why borrow it from Xǔ Yóu?

Circular illumination versus partial obsession,

Guō Xiàng observed the mind of non-reliance,

This is merely one thing among common customs,

If an external minister replaces the internal master,
then he has the name of a ruler but not the reality of one.

Master Zhuāng (莊生) resonates beautiful sounds in the seven chapters,
establishing this literary style for later (two) generations.
Repetitive language extensively explores the path of the profound,
while his work develops (three) narratives that are rich in language.
Although he discusses non-being, his arguments are valuable,
and his teachings are never empty pronouncements.
Yet his writing is easy to read,
while its essence is difficult to discern.
Those who engage with it but fail to grasp its meaning
may have reason to find fault with it.

he greatly cites Huì Zi's 惠子 eloquence.

The Gūyè State is in the sea,
belonging to Liègūyè,
surrounded by mountains to the southwest.
In the "Huángdì" chapter of the *Lièzǐ*,
Mount Liègūyè is in the Hé River islet in the sea,
consistent with the "Northern Classic Within the Seas."
(The following text, about a divine person on the mountain,
is generally similar to that in the *Zhuāngzǐ*.
This sufficiently proves that the sound and meaning, saying that Gūyè is in the Northern Sea, are not mistaken.)
Yīn Jìngshùn of the Táng dynasty, in his *Commentary on Lièzǐ*, quotes the *Shānhǎijīng*, saying:
"The Gūyè State is in the sea,
surrounded by mountains to the southwest.
Traveling a hundred *lǐ* south from the state by water,
one reaches Mount Gūyè.
Traveling another three hundred and eighty *lǐ* southwest,
one reaches Mount Gūyè."
Guō (Pú) says it is on the sea traversed by the Hé River.
It means that the various Mount Gūyè are remotely visible in rows between the sea and the Hé River.
This differs from the current version of the *Shānhǎijīng*.
The "Geography" section of the *Suí Shū* states,
"In Línfén, there is Mount Gūyè."
This is the Gūyè mentioned in the "Eastern Classic of Mountains."
What Zhuāng Zǐ called Mount Gūyè
on the north bank of the Fén River is this.
According to Qín Shì'ēn's annotations to the Lièzǐ and supplemental notes,
the Gūyè [mountain] near Línfén
is the present-day Nine-Holed Mountain west of Píngyáng Prefecture.
There is nothing called north or south Gūyè either before, after, left, or right of it.
Proving this with Yīn's glosses,
the two sections on north and south Gūyè in the "Eastern Mountains Classic"
should be below the "Northern Classic of Regions Within the Seas" and "Mountains Surrounding the Southwest."
There must be a ring of various Gūyè mountains
before they can be named as the Gūyè [mountains] together.
Moreover, the Shānhǎijīng that Yīn relied on was a Tang dynasty version.
Supposedly, the original ancient version was like this.
I don't know when it was omitted in copying
and inserted after the section on Mount Gūyè in the "Eastern Mountains Classic,"
thus becoming the present version.
Fortunately, there are the glosses on the Lièzǐ,
which can correct the errors in the Shānhǎijīng.
Furthermore, Zhuāng Zǐ mentions Gūyè twice,
once in the Northern Sea
and once near Línfén,
thus avoiding confusion of them into one.
(Bì Yuán's annotations to the Shānhǎijīng quote Zhuāng Zǐ,
mistakenly combining them into one.
) Although the texts are all allegories,
the locations of the mountain names
are all certainly and reliably attested,
so there should be no harm in differentiating and verifying them.

【Three】【Note】Ah, the mind of the sage
reaches the ultimate meeting point of the two primal forces,
and exhausts the wondrous numbers of all things.
Therefore, he can embody transformation and unite with change,
going nowhere that is not permissible,
overflowing and blending with all things,
with nothing being not so.
The world seeks me because of disorder,
but I have no (predetermined) mind.
If I truly have no (predetermined) mind,
then why should I not respond to the world?
Thus, he who embodies the profound and attains the ultimate subtlety,
through which he connects and understands the nature of all things,
and molds and transforms the civilization of the world,
to achieve the reputation of Yáo and Shùn,
always achieves it by acting through non-action.
How could one, exhausted, wearying one's spirit and laboring one's thoughts,
treat affairs as affairs,
and then be capable of it!

[Eight] [Commentary] Yáo's having no use for governing the world
is like a Yuè person having no use for a ceremonial cap.
Yet, he who abandons the world
is indeed the one whom the world honors.
Although the world honors Yáo,
Yáo never truly possessed the world,
therefore he serenely lost it,
and constantly wandered in a state of absolute darkness,
Although he sits enthroned above all things, he has never ceased to be carefree.
The words of these four men are probably allegorical,
to make clear that Yáo is not simply Yáo.
Indeed, Yáo is truly unfathomable;
his actions are those of Yáo.
Judging the unfathomable from his actions,
the inner and outer realms are different territories,
which is not at all surprising.
The world only sees Yáo as Yáo,
how could they know his unfathomable nature!
Therefore, to seek the four men overseas while relying on the perceived Yáo,
and consequently saying that he is simply following the trends with things,
is to miss the reason for his carefree state.
However, they do not know that the place nearest to the ultimate distance is the place of obedience,
and the place where the highest things converge is actually low.
If one is fiercely determined to regard exclusive loftiness as the ultimate without leveling oneself to mundane burdens,
then one is merely a recluse of the mountains and valleys,
and is not without dependencies.
How can such a person speak of the ultimate limit and roam endlessly!

People uniformly judge based on what they see;

For example, in the *Shǐjì: Sīmǎ Xiàngrú Zhuàn*, it says, "Shì xuànmián ér wú jiàn xī" (視眩眠而無見兮, I see but see nothing in a dizzy spell) and "jí hóng yǎomiǎo ér xuànmǐn xī" (及紅杳渺而眩湣兮, and the red is distant and indistinct, causing dizziness), these are all examples.
The characters all have similar meanings and pronunciations.
Lù’s 冥 (míng) is pronounced wǔ pián qiē.
And Xú’s 瞑 (míng) is pronounced wǔ yán qiē.
However, Yán Shīgǔ’s commentary on the *Hànshū* says 冥 (míng) is pronounced mò jiàn fǎn.

Suǒ Yǐn in the *Shǐjì* quotes Sū Lín saying 湣 (mǐn) is pronounced mǐ.
The rhyme categories are all the same.
(In ancient times, there were no light labial sounds,
wǔ and mò had the same initial consonant.)
Only the tones (level vs. oblique) are different.
冥 (míng) and 窅 (yǎo) also have similar meanings,

Guō, in his commentary here, uses the character 冥 (míng) four times in succession,

Regarding "zhī zhǒng (之種)," pronounce "zhǒng (種)" as "zhāng yǒng fǎn (章勇反)."

【Three】【Commentary】 Pōu,
means to divide and cut.
Piáo,
means ladle.
Hù luò,
means flat and shallow.
Xiāo rán,
means empty and large.
Póu,
means to break.
If used to hold water,
it is fragile and cannot support itself;
if divided and cut into ladles,
it is flat and shallow and cannot hold much.
People consider it useless,
so they break it and discard it.
This is a criticism of Zhuāngzǐ's words,
that they do not address the urgent needs of the time,

【Seven】 【Commentary】The gōng and shāng tones of sound, though changing in thousands of ways,
in singing in harmony, whether high or low,
all correspond to what they receive and each fulfills its role.
【Subcommentary】Líng means
a small breeze.
Piāo means
a strong wind.
Yú yóng are
all sounds of wind blowing through trees, following one after another.
Thus, the cool and clear breeze, líng líng,
when harmonized, is small;
the violent and swift wind, piāo fēng,
when harmonized, is large;
each corresponds to what it receives,
with no superiority or inferiority,
to illustrate how all things naturally receive their qi.

None is specifically Heaven,

【Commentary】Heaven,
is the collective name for all things,
another name for the natural,
how could it refer to the azure sky!
Therefore, the music of Heaven,
how could it be a separate thing?
It is just like the many holes of the bi bamboo connecting to things of the living kind.
Investigating who it is that generates all life,
it is essentially nothing.
Therefore, externally it does not depend on things,
internally it does not rely on the self;
it comes into being of itself,
transforming alone.
Therefore, Guō (郭)注 says,
"That which is so of itself
is called natural (tiānrán)."
Thus, speaking in terms of "natural"
is to clarify its being natural.
And to speak of blowing on the ten thousand things differently:
moreover, the wind is a single entity,
while the apertures are myriad and diverse.
Although they differ in size,
each conforms to what it receives;
all follow their own knowledge.
How could they rely on anything else?
This is the music of Heaven.
Thus, knowing that spring brings forth and summer fosters growth,
that the eyes see and the ears hear,
drawing near to what is within the body,
Entrusting things to afar,
all do not know the reason for it,
all cannot discern what makes it so.
If they are left to themselves,
each will have its proper share and be content,
acting according to its nature,
not guided by mind or intellect,
this is what is meant by "nurturing them and poisoning them,"
this is the grand meaning of the music of Heaven.

However, sorrow and joy are weighty,

Therefore, with joy, the heart generates delight;
with happiness, it manifests in dancing and excitement.
With anger, there is immediate resentment;
with sorrow, the whole body wails in grief.
With worry, one speculates about the future;
with lament, one sighs over the past.
With change, one alters old affairs;
with timidity (*zhé*), one is subdued and unable to stand up straight.
With frivolousness (*yáo*), one is light, unrestrained, and agitated;
with dissipation (*yì*), one is extravagant, luxurious, and unrestrained.
With incitement (*qǐ*), one expands and opens up desires and passions;
with affectation (*tài*), one is coquettish, licentious, and seductive.
The minds and consciousnesses of sentient beings
are endlessly changing and transforming;
to speak briefly,
there are these twelve.
If one examines and observes them carefully,
the nature of things will then be seen.

*Hóngliè* (淮南子)'s *Yuándào* chapter,
Now, a well fish cannot be spoken to about the vastness

"The well is foul; one shoots small fish."

Later people, because this chapter contains the phrase "well frog,"

Since this change was made,

and no longer understands the metaphor of the "well fish."

in the midst of the vast sea.
He carefully observed the boundless great ravines,
and then looked down upon the narrow and inferior small river.
Having realized the limitations of his dwelling place,
therefore, it is possible to speak of the vast and unobstructed principles.
[III] [Elucidation]: Wěilǘ (尾閭) is
the place where seawater is discharged.
It is located to the east of the blue sea.
In that place, there is a rock,
40,000 *lǐ* wide
and 40,000 *lǐ* thick,
residing beneath the tails of hundreds of rivers and forming a gate-like gathering (閭族),
therefore, it is called Wěilǘ (尾閭).
When seawater pours onto it, it immediately burns,
it is also called Wòjiāo (沃焦).
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* (山海經) says,
Yì (羿) shot down nine suns,
which fell and became Wòjiāo (沃焦).
This saying is absurd and exaggerated;
I will not record it in detail.
There is little rain in the spring but much rain in the autumn.
Yáo zāo shuǐ ér Tāng zāo hàn.
Therefore, the sea as a thing,
ten thousand streams flow into it without filling it,
the Wòjiāo drains it without emptying it,
spring and autumn do not change its amount,
floods and droughts do not know its increase or decrease.
Discussing its greatness,
it far surpasses the flow of the (Sea) [River] (six),
the difference in superiority and inferiority is vast,
how can one speak of its quantity!
【Explanation of the Text】“Wěilǘ,” Cuī says:
a stream name east of the sea.
Sīmǎ says:
it is that which drains seawater outwards.
“Xiè zhī,” read xī liè, and also yǔ shì.
yòu yǔ shì fǎn.

【Four】【Commentary】 Exhausting the measure of the hundreds of rivers and suspending it in the [Yellow] River,
the River suspending it in the sea,
and the sea suspending it in Heaven and Earth,
then each has its own measure.
This is a way of expressing oneself,
seemingly suggesting that by observing the great, one can understand the small,
but upon examining its meaning, it is not so.
What troubles the world
is inequality.
Therefore, those with a large body [self-satisfiedly] consider those with a small body to have nothing left over,
and those with a small substance stubbornly consider those with a large body to be completely sufficient.
It is because of this that superiors and inferiors boast and exaggerate,
losing themselves in bowing and looking up,
and this is what perplexes the people.
Those who are perplexed seek correctness,
and the way to correct them is to first exhaust their differences and follow what they call them.
What they call great is complete sufficiency,
therefore even an autumn hair cannot add to Heaven and Earth;
what they call small is having nothing left over,
Therefore, even the smallest thing, like an autumn down feather, cannot surpass the scope of Heaven and Earth.
Then, those who are confused have a way to return to clarity,
each knowing their limit,
things being content with their lot,
and those who wander freely use their own inherent pace to roam in the field of self-attainment.
This is the reason why Zhuāng Zǐ issues his virtuous words.
If we were to follow the arguments of those who are confused,
turning to using small and large to overthrow each other,
then there would be no end to the overthrowing.
As for those who see the great and are uneasy with the small,
and view the little and consider themselves to have much,
they will rush about in the competition of winning and losing, assisting the pride and boasting of the people under Heaven.
How could they understand the meaning of Master Zhuāng!
[Commentary] Cún (存) means "to exist," "to be present."
Xī (奚) means "what," "how."
In covering and supporting all things, nothing is greater than Heaven and Earth;
in distributing breath and generating transformation, nothing is greater than Yīn and Yáng.
Therefore, if Hé Ruò (海若) compares his form to Heaven and Earth,
there would be no rank or degree to entrust to it.
Saying he receives breath from Yīn and Yáng,
then Yīn and Yáng are merely one thing among many.
Therefore, entrusting it to things as an analogy
is like a small tree or small stone on Mount Tài;
and how much does Hé Ruò (海若) matter in the principles of Heaven, in terms of quantity?
Things each have their measure,
so how can he be satisfied with himself!

People often suspect that the two characters "dà lǜ" (大率)

"Shuài" (率) was mistakenly written as "zú" (卒),

"Calculate" and "dà lǜ" (大率)

hence it is said they contended and became kings.

When the time calls for yielding,
one should respond with Yáo and Shùn.

should not be rigidly adhered to.

do they truly "see" because they strive to see?

so they try to "know" through striving to know;
they do not understand that seeing comes from its own seeing,
so they try to "see" through striving to see;
they do not understand that life comes from its own living,
so they will try to "live" through striving to live.

【校】(1) *Quèwù* cites the ancient Jiangnan collection edition of this sentence as "Few people do not act wrongly to achieve joy."
Zhòng Ní said:
"There are two great prohibitions in the world:
The first,
Is fate;
The second,
Is righteousness.
Your love for your parents,
Is fate,
And cannot be dispelled from the heart;
A minister's service to his lord,
Is righteousness,
There is nowhere that is not the lord's,
There is nowhere to escape between heaven and earth.
This is what is called the great precept.
Therefore, serving one's parents
without choosing the place to be content with them,
is the utmost filial piety.
Serving one's ruler,
without choosing the task to be content with it,
is the height of loyalty.
Serving one's own heart,
not easily letting sorrow or joy affect one's countenance,
knowing that there is nothing to be done about it, and accepting it as fate,
is the perfection of virtue.
Those who are ministers and sons,
certainly have things they cannot avoid.
Pursuing the true nature of affairs and forgetting oneself,
how could they have time to delight in life and hate death!
The Master's conduct is indeed exemplary!
[Commentary 1] "Precept"
means law.
Within the universe,
there are extremely many teachings and laws,
but speaking of what is essential and important,
nothing surpasses these two matters.
The meaning and purpose of these two matters
are fully explained in the following text.
[Commentary 2] Naturally bound together,
and cannot be unbound.
[Commentary] When a filial son serves his parents,
he exhausts himself in love and reverence.
This nature and destiny
originate from nature,
and the center follows and complies.
Therefore, it cannot be unraveled.
【Third】【Commentary】When a thousand people gather,
if one person is not the leader,
it will disintegrate into chaos.
Therefore, having many capable individuals cannot equate to having many rulers,
but lacking capable individuals does not mean one can be without a ruler.
This is the way of Heaven and humanity,
an inevitable necessity.
【Elucidation】The relationship between ruler and subject, superior and subordinate,
is a principle that is inherently inevitable.
Therefore, a loyal minister serves his ruler,
and dies to fulfill his integrity.
This is a matter of shared duty and righteousness,
and not related to innate nature.
However, although the universe is vast,
there has never been a country without a ruler.
If there is guilt or blame,
where can one escape their sins?
Therefore, one should follow orders and act immediately,
without bothering about advancing or retreating.
【Fourth】【Commentary】If one can escape their ruler and abandon their parents,
then there is nothing to be warned about.
【Elucidation】Before making a commitment, the most important principle is the moral obligation to one's ruler and parents.
【Fifth】【Elucidation】A filial son cares for his parents,
striving to be agreeable and compliant.
Seeking officialdom and salary,
he does not choose high or low positions,
but is content with what he encounters.
This is called perfect filial piety.
【Sixth】【Elucidation】Treating relatives with propriety and serving one's lord,
requires wholeheartedly devoting oneself to loyalty and integrity.
to conduct affairs regardless of ease or danger,
and to accept them as fate—
how could one pick and choose advantages and disadvantages
before acting accordingly!
One who can do this
is the epitome of a loyal subject.
[Seventh Commentator] Knowing that what cannot be helped is fate and being content with it
leads to neither sorrow nor joy,
so how can one easily change one's course!
Therefore, accepting what one encounters as fate without applying one's mind to it,
and blending into oneness with the ultimate rightness without worrying about good or ill fortune,
even when dealing with ordinary people,
one will find nothing that is not suitable,
how much more so with one's ruler and parents!
[Commentary] A follower of the Dao who sets his mind at ease,
understands that conformity and nonconformity are no different,
and realizes that gain and loss are one and the same.
Therefore, when facing situations that evoke sorrow or joy,
they do not change their course easily,
knowing that poverty and success are inevitable.
How can human emotions control them!
Therefore, by setting their minds at ease and accepting fate,
Does not deviate from the principles of Heaven.
If not a person of utmost virtue and profound understanding (zhìrén xuándé),
who could be like this!

Guō (郭) suspects that the character "戕" (qiāng) is missing below.
In the Guǎngyùn, entry for the eleventh "唐" (Táng), under "戕" (qiāng), it says:
"Qiāngkē,"

The commentary in the Hànshū (漢書) Geography Record for the Zāngkē (牂牁) Commandery says:
"牂戕" (zāngqiāng),
is a mooring stake for boats.
Therefore, Guō's version, using "戕" (qiāng), is the "戕" (qiāng) of "戕柯" (qiāngkē),
which is similar in shape and meaning to "杙" (yì), but different in sound;
its sound is qiě yáng fǎn (且羊反),
so it is clear that it is "戕" (qiāng) and not "杙" (yì).

"is the name of an acupoint,"

The bones on both sides

Therefore, the bones meet at Dàzhù.
According to this,

and it is also located between the Dàzhuī vertebra,
hence it is called "neck vertebra."

【8】【Commentary】A divine person is useless to things,
but each thing is able to use itself.
They attribute merit and fame to the talent of the group,
merge with things without a trace,
and therefore avoid the harm of human idleness,
and reside in the reality of constant beauty.
This is one whose virtue is "branch-detached."
[Commentary] To be deformed in body
is akin to forgetting one's body;
to be deficient in virtue
is akin to forgetting one's virtue.
And what is more, to be deformed, disabled, and ill,
is merely to forget one's body;
since he is not a sage,
he is therefore unable to forget his virtue.
Now, one who forgets virtue
has wisdom that encompasses all things, yet turns his wisdom to seeming foolishness;
his brightness rivals the three luminaries (sun, moon, and stars), yet he returns his brightness to seeming darkness.
Therefore, he can achieve success without claiming credit,
act without relying on his own power,
and attribute merit and fame to all talents.
He merges with things and leaves no trace.
This is one who forgets virtue.
Even one who forgets his body is sufficient to nourish himself for his entire life
and avoid the harms of the world.
How much more so one who forgets virtue!
The degree of superiority or inferiority, shallowness or depth,
is therefore not to be spoken of in the same breath.
Thus, one knows that to be deficient in virtue
is only possible for a sage.
[Collations] (1) The Shìdétáng edition lacks the two characters "ér yóu" (而遊, and roam).
(2) The character "bò" (簸, to winnow) is changed based on the Shìdétáng edition.
(3) According to the commentary (释文), it does not state that "jīng" 精 is pronounced as "qǔ" 取.
What it refers to as a single pronunciation
refers to the character "bò" 播,
Therefore, it is said that the word should be taken as a number.
Guō Shuō's explanation is greatly mistaken.
(4) The character "shì" (恃) is changed based on the commentary and the Shìdétáng edition.
Kǒngzǐ went to Chǔ.
The madman of Chǔ, Jiē Yú, wandered by his gate and said:
"Phoenix, oh phoenix,
how is it that virtue is in decline!
The coming age is not to be waited for,
the past age is not to be pursued!
When the world is on the right path,
sages achieve success;
when the world is without the right path,
sages are born.
In these times,
one can barely avoid punishment.
Blessings are as light as a feather,
but no one knows how to carry them;
disasters are as heavy as the earth,
but no one knows how to avoid them.
Enough, enough,
govern people with virtue!
Perilous, perilous,
to draw a line on the ground and rush along it!
Confused, confused,
do not harm my steps!
My steps (1) are crooked,
do not harm my feet!"
exhausting the appropriateness of understanding and adapting.
The rise and fall of the world
are too insignificant to be noticed,
therefore it is said, "how is it".
[Commentary] "How is it"
is the same as "how is it?"
Shì (適),
means "to go to."
At this time, Kǒngzǐ (孔子) went from Lǔ (魯) to Chǔ (楚)
and stayed at the state guesthouse.
In Chǔ (楚) there was a worthy man,
named Lù (陸),
his given name was Tōng (通),
his style name was Jiēyú (接輿),
who knew Kǒngzǐ (孔子) was traveling and seeking employment,
so he sang and satirized him.
"Oh phoenix, oh phoenix!"
He therefore lamented the sage,
comparing him to the auspicious bird that appears in response to good omens.
If there is the Dao, he should appear;
if there is no Dao, he should remain hidden.
How can he cherish this sagely virtue
and go to a declining and chaotic state?
【Second Commentary】 The essence lies in exhausting the appropriateness of the immediate situation.
【Commentary】 In the coming age,
there may be a ruler who cherishes the Dao and is worthy of being employed.
Time and fate race by,
therefore one cannot wait.
At the time of going,
the rulers Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜),
their transformations have been long past,
and cannot be found.
Strive to accord with what is appropriate for the present time,
and do not trouble yourself with looking forward and backward.
【3】【Commentary】 Entrust matters to themselves,
and the principles will naturally come into being.
The coming into being is not due to me,
how could it be that for the sake of order or chaos, one should change one's integrity?
Those who govern seek success on their own,
therefore, they abandon fixed outcomes and are not defeated;
those who cause chaos seek survival on their own,
therefore, they forget about life and do not die.
【Elucidation】 A ruler who possesses the Way,
in an era of peace and enlightenment,
the sage promotes the Way and imparts teachings,
achieving [great things] for the world.
If the time meets a foolish ruler,
and fate belongs to a time of decline and disorder,
it is appropriate to preserve life and avoid harm,
concealing one's brilliance and hiding one's tracks.
【Explanation of Text】《豈為》 (qǐ wéi) is pronounced yú wěi fǎn.
《治亂》(zhì luàn) is pronounced zhí lì fǎn.
The same applies below.
【4】【Commentary】 Without looking forward or backward,
but fully embracing the opportunities of the present,
being subtly in harmony with the times,
Only then can the subtlety be fully realized,
and punishment be avoided.
【Commentary】方 (fāng),
is like 當 (dāng).
Now is a time of chaos and disorder,
truly belonging to the declining Zhou dynasty.
To act cautiously and speak humbly
is barely enough to avoid punishment.
To then seek to grasp at opportunities and accept appointments,
isn't that foolish?
These are the words of Jiē Yú,
ridiculing Kǒngzǐ.
【Explanatory Notes】《僅》is pronounced jìn.
【Five】【Commentary】Feet are able to walk and are allowed to,
hands are able to hold and are entrusted to,
ears listen to what they hear,
eyes see what they see,
know when to stop at what is not known,
are able to stop at what cannot be done,
use what one is able to use,
do what one is able to do,
indulge one's inner nature and have no trace of concern for what is beyond one's proper role.
This is the easiest form of non-action (wúwéi).
Those who practice non-action (wúwéi) and yet do not preserve their lives,
have never existed;
and lives preserved that do not result in blessings,
such a principle has not been heard.
Therefore, as for blessings,
they are exactly what was previously called "wholeness";
they are not borrowed from external things.
How could they have the weight of a feather placed on them?
To act according to one's nature,
and not to overstep the mark in one's actions,
is the easiest thing in the world.
To lift what lifts itself,
to carry what carries itself,
is the lightest thing in the world.
However, knowing uses boundlessness to injure nature,
and the mind uses desires and aversions to disrupt truth.
Therefore, they abandon this effortless ease of wúwéi 無為 and practice the difficult exertion of yǒu wéi 有為,
discarding the intrinsic lightness of self-lifting and taking up the extrinsic heaviness of carrying something else.
This is a common problem in the world.
[Explanation of the Text] "Zhì Yì" (至易, Extremely Easy) is pronounced with the "chǐ" (豉) reversal.
The same applies below.
"Zhī Yǐ" (知以, Knowing Uses) is pronounced "zhì" (智).
"Yù Wù" (欲惡, Desires and Aversions) is pronounced "wū lù" (烏路) reversal.
[Sixth Chapter Commentary] To act based on one's internal nature,
even bearing ten thousand *jūn* (鈞) would not feel heavy;
but when external things are attached,
even if they weigh less than a *zī zhū* (錙銖),
one cannot bear the burden.
Acting internally
is a blessing,
so blessings are extremely light;
acting externally
is a disaster,
so disasters are extremely heavy.
Disasters are extremely heavy, yet no one knows how to avoid them;
this is the great delusion of the world.
[Commentary] Vision, hearing, knowing, and ability
seem to have boundaries.
Stopping within those boundaries,
kěyǐ quán shēng; one can preserve life;
qiú qí fēn wài, if one seeks beyond these boundaries,
bì zāo yāo zhé. one will inevitably encounter premature death.
quán shēng suǒyǐ wéi fú, Preserving life is the means to attain blessings,
yāo zhé suǒyǐ wéi huò. and premature death is the means to bring about calamity.
ér fēn nèi zhī fú, The blessings within one's boundaries,
qīng yú hóng máo, are lighter than a swan's feather.
tān jìng zhī tú, Greedy and competitive people
bù zhī zài zhī zài jǐ; do not know that they are carried within themselves;
fēn wài zhī huò, the calamities beyond one's boundaries,
chóng yú hòu dì, are heavier than the thick earth.
zhí mí zhī tú, Stubborn and deluded people
bù zhī bì zhī qù shēn. do not know to avoid them and keep them away from themselves.
cǐ gài liú sú zhī cháng huàn zhě yě, This is generally the common ailment of the vulgar masses.
gù jì Kǒng Lù yǐ zhāng qí lěi yě. Therefore, it is entrusted to Kǒng [Zǐ] and Lù [Jì] to reveal its burden.

【qī】【zhù】 fú huà dì ér shǐ rén xún zhī, [Seven][Commentary] Now, if you draw a line on the ground and make people follow it,
qí jì bù kě yǎn yǐ; the traces cannot be concealed;
yǒu qí jǐ ér lín wù, if you have your own self and confront things,
yǔ wù bù míng yǐ.
Therefore, a great person does not use my brilliance to illuminate others but allows them to shine on their own;
does not use my virtue to oversee people but entrusts virtue to them for their own gain (sān).
Therefore, one can thoroughly penetrate all things and profoundly unite self and others,
indistinctly becoming one with the world and experiencing inner and outer blessings equally.
【Commentary】Yǐ,
stop.
Dài,
dangerous.
Zhòng Ní was born at the end of the declining Zhōu dynasty,
during a time of moral decay.
Holding onto the vestiges of sagehood,
he traveled to various states seeking employment,
frequently encountering rejection and expulsion,
and being repeatedly criticized and slandered.
Therefore, he repeatedly said, "Better to stop and not travel!"
If one were to use the Five Virtues to oversee the common people,
abandoning oneself to emulate external things,
one would inevitably endanger oneself.
It would be like drawing tracks on the ground
and making people chase after them,
wasting clever effort in vain,
with no way to conceal the deception.
To lead others with oneself
has the same meaning.
【Explanation of the Text】"Huà Dì" (drawing tracks on the ground) is pronounced huò.
【Eight】【Annotation】Mí Yáng,
is like losing one's yang.
It is like losing the sun.
If one relies on singularity after losing the sun,
and is not swayed by external things,
then my actions will be complete.
If everyone in the world completes their "I,"
then all who call themselves "I" will be complete.

[Three] [Annotation] Being useful means cooperating with others to achieve merit,
it is the same with people.
Being useless means preserving one's own life.
To cut one's own flesh to benefit the world,
Is something the world knows.
To enable the people to preserve themselves while both sides benefit,
Is to unknowingly realize the wonder within oneself.
[Commentary] The catalpa, cypress, tangerine, and pomelo,
Grease-fire, cinnamon, and lacquer,
These are useful.
The trees on the curved roads,
The wood of Shāngqiū,
The white-browed ox,
The pig with its nostrils facing upwards,
These are useless.
But people all flaunt their talents to appear useful,
And do not know that to dismember their virtue is to be useful in being useless.
Therefore, Guō's annotation says,
Being useful means cooperating with others to achieve merit,
Being useless means preserving one's own life.
【Explanation of Text】《Mán Rán》亡本反 (wáng běn fǎn).
Inner Chapters, Virtue Made Manifest, Chapter Five
【One】【Commentary】Virtue filling within,
responding to things outwardly,
inner and outer merging mysteriously,
is as reliable as a talisman, thus abandoning its form.
【Explanation of Text】Cuī (崔) says:
This is abandoning form and discarding knowledge,
using virtue as the evidence of its reality.
【Corrections】（一）物應依趙諫議本改："（Yī）wù yìng yī Zhào Jiànyì běn gǎi" (The response to things should be emended according to the Zhao Jianyi edition).
In Lǔ (魯) there was a cripple named Wáng Tái (王駘) [One],
those who followed him were as numerous as those who followed Zhòng Ní (仲尼) [Two].
Cháng Jì (常季) asked Zhòng Ní (仲尼), saying:
"Wáng Tái (王駘),
a cripple,
those who follow him divide Lǔ (魯) equally with you, Master [Three].
He does not teach when standing,
nor does he discuss when sitting,
they go empty,
and return full [Four].
Does he possess teaching without words,
and completion of the heart without form [Five]?
What kind of person is he [Six]?"
【One】【Commentary】His surname is Wáng (王),
his name is Tái (駘),
he is a man of Lǔ (魯).
To have one foot cut off is called "wù (兀)".
